content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Gospel' (Greek euangelion, 'good news') primarily denotes the message of salvation accomplished by God through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ — the announcement that God has acted in Christ to forgive sin, reconcile humanity to himself, and inaugurate his kingdom, received by faith. It is less a symbol than a technical term for the core Christian proclamation (kerygma).","primary_basis":["1 Corinthians 15:1-4 (Paul's summary definition: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised)","Romans 1:16-17 (the gospel as the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes)","Mark 1:1 ('The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God')","Mark 1:14-15 (Jesus proclaiming the gospel of God: the kingdom is at hand, repent and believe)","Isaiah 52:7 (the herald of good news announcing God's reign, background text)","Luke 4:18-19 (Jesus anointed to proclaim good news to the poor, citing Isaiah 61)","Galatians 1:6-9 (there is one true gospel, not to be altered)","Ephesians 1:13 (the gospel of your salvation)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The gospel as the announcement of the kingdom of God — God's reign breaking into history through Jesus — with personal salvation as one component of a broader cosmic and social restoration (emphasized in kingdom-centered, missional, and much recent New Testament scholarship, e.g., N.T. Wright).","basis":["Mark 1:14-15","Matthew 4:23; 9:35 ('the gospel of the kingdom')","Luke 4:18-19","Isaiah 52:7"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"'Gospel' as a literary designation: the four canonical narratives (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) recounting Jesus' life, death, and resurrection — a genre label rather than the message itself.","basis":["Mark 1:1 (title usage)","Early church usage (2nd-century titling, e.g., 'the Gospel according to Matthew')"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Dispensationalist distinction between multiple gospels — e.g., the 'gospel of the kingdom' preached to Israel versus the 'gospel of the grace of God' preached by Paul to the church — treating them as distinct messages for distinct dispensations.","basis":["Matthew 4:23; 24:14","Acts 20:24","Galatians 2:7 (gospel to the circumcised vs. uncircumcised)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The gospel as a counter-imperial proclamation: euangelion deliberately echoes Roman imperial announcements of the emperor's accession or victories, so declaring Jesus' gospel is a political claim that Jesus, not Caesar, is Lord (emphasized in empire-critical scholarship).","basis":["Mark 1:1 compared with the Priene calendar inscription about Augustus","Romans 1:1-4","Philippians 2:9-11; Acts 17:7"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Law/Gospel distinction in Lutheran and Reformed theology: 'Gospel' functions as one of two modes of God's word — pure promise and grace, contrasted with the demands and condemnation of the Law.","basis":["Romans 3:19-24","Galatians 3:10-14","John 1:17"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Social-gospel or liberationist reading: the gospel is primarily good news of liberation for the poor and oppressed, entailing social and economic justice in the present age.","basis":["Luke 4:18-19","Luke 6:20","Matthew 25:31-46"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"'Gospel' is unusual among terms submitted for symbolic analysis because it is not primarily a symbol (like 'lamb' or 'leaven') but a defined theological term with a broad, stable consensus core: the good news of salvation through Christ's death and resurrection, anchored especially in 1 Corinthians 15:1-4 and Romans 1:16. The alternative readings listed are mostly differences of emphasis or scope (kingdom-centered, law/gospel, political, social) rather than denials of the core. Genuine disagreement exists mainly at the margins: dispensationalist multiple-gospel schemes and strongly politicized or purely social redefinitions are minority positions. If an author's book assigns 'Gospel' a materially different or esoteric symbolic meaning (e.g., an allegorical code detached from the Christ-event), that would diverge from recognizable consensus."}
